The Hidden Cost of Food

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
An estimated fourteen million South Africans are going to bed hungry everyday. Economists are projecting a turn for the better with food prices, but is that a reality at the tills?

Unique Selling Point:
The turn of the year 2017 has shown positive signs of food prices dropping in South Africa with economists projecting the food inflation to decline up to 7% by midyear. Consumers however, still have to dig deep into their pockets to put food on the table with prices of basic nutritional staples not reflecting the anticipated consumer relief at the supermarkets while the poor, in fact, are further stifled.

Summary:
Severe draught, the weakening Rand and an increased rate of imported foods have all plagued the South African food economy in the past two years. The cost of food prices climbed to almost 30% in 2016, putting ordinary South Africans against the ropes just to feed their families. A good rain spell in the recent months has however improved the Agricultural sector in South Africa with Grain industry expected to produce a surplus in 2017. This will help reduce the price of food products such as maize, which is a major staple, particularly in low- income households. Maize has already shown a downtrend since January 2017 and this is expected to impact majorly on food inflation in South Africa and consumers are supposed to be feeling the decrease already.

On the contrary the general projection of food inflation has risen by 10% y/y in South Africans and consumers are still paying more for a basic nutritional diet in their house with other staples such as meat, sugar and cooking oil still at an all time high. The recent downgrade of our economy to junk status coupled with the less 5% salary increases across the working class and the social grants, maintains a gloomy picture for the consumer, especially the poor.

In this follow up piece, we unpack the discrepancy between the positive economic outlook and the negative reality hitting the consumer at the super markets. Experts shed light on what is influencing the current food inflation and what the ordinary South African consumer should brace them selves for.


Further information:
According to world bank surveys, South Africa is one of the most unequal societies in the world, sitting at number 2, when it comes to poverty and inequality, with our CEO's being the 7th highest paid globally.

Vuyokazi from SPII (Studies in Poverty and Inequality Institute) puts into perspective what an average low incomme household and ones that rely on social grants spend on food. Based on their research, how does inflation work against a social grant recipient whom their annual increase does not equate to the annual increases in food inflation.” The standard of living the poor are expected to live on is degrading” She backs this up the Trend Analysis of essential food and non-food basket they conduct at the SPII.

Last year we tracked the food basket from PACSA nutritional basket in 2016. Julie Smith from PACSA outlines how their food basket of nutritional and non-nutritional food items has increased on a m/m basis as well as y/y to date. Julie also breaks down the inadequacy of the suggested national minimum wage of R3500 by government compared to the cost of a nutritional food basket of a family consisting of five people according to the PACSA research and food barometer.

To unpack this at a broader economic level, economist, Lesiba Mothata from Investment Solutions, talks to us about the general effect of inflation on the middle class and low-income earners. Lesiba also unpacks the level of inequality in South Africa and why especially the low-income household will feel the brunt of an economic downgrade in the country. Who will absorb the high interest rates in the country now that we are at a junk status? Most importantly Lesiba will put into perspective on a larger scale the reason why the supposed decline and positive outlook on food inflation doesn’t reflect at the shops for the consumer.

Viccy Baker of Price Watch believes there is a discrepancy in the increases of certain foods from certain brands. According to Viccy some of the brands’ are unnecessarily high and the rate in which they increase suggests price fixing and profiteering. She takes us on stroll in the supermarket as she discusses some of the foods she used to buy for cheaper and they have since accelerated to almost twice their former price. Based on the food items they track at Price Watch, she helps us compare the national statistics and inflation rates to what they have calculated.

In conclusion, the experts, Wandile and Lesiba give us an actual figure breakdown of what the food inflation projection is standing at and also a little advice for the consumer and whether they should be more cautious with their spending, or better days are near. What is the forecast for the near future, is it positive, or are factors such as an economic downgrade going send back to a 20%+ food inflation rate?

Press Release:


The turn of the year 2017 has shown positive signs of food prices dropping in South Africa with economists projecting the food inflation to decline up to 7% by midyear. Consumers however, still have to dig deep into their pockets to put food on the table with prices of basic nutritional staples not reflecting the anticipated consumer relief at the supermarkets while the poor, in fact, are further stifled.

Script:


Bongani: The rich get richer and the poor get poorer, we know the saying. [12:59:44.19] In SA, it's particularly true. We remain one of the most unequal societies in the world. [12:59:50.11] Millions go to bed hungry whilst a few people are coining it.

VO: In a recent Bloomberg study, South African CEO's from the top 40 listed companies on the JSE were found to be the 7th highest paid in the world, earning on average 7.14 million dollars per year. PACSA Advocacy and research co-ordinator, Dr Julie Smith says, we are perpetuating an unsustainable economy.

Julie: If you compare that to the national minimum wage figure which will provide workers R20 an hour, it's only within this framework that we can start seeing this extreme level of inequality

VO: Vuyokazi Futshane from the Studies in Poverty and Inequality Institute, says that South Africa's economic power still lies in the hands of a minority.

Vuyo: It's also very racialised because the fact that when it comes to poverty and equality, it's a reality that black households, especially black female households are affected by poverty the most.

VO: The median wage for a black South African worker is R2 900,00 per month which typically supports a household of 4, this translates to a poverty wage that is way below the upper bound poverty line of R1077,00 per person per month. Would the proposed national minimum wage of R3500,00 bring significant relief?

Julie: Even if we can sign an agreement around a national minimum wage, workers are still going to be locked, and now in institutionalised poverty.

VO: Agri Economist Tinashe Kapuya says that the poor are trapped in a downward spiral of unaffordability.

Tinashe: we are progressively becoming poorer, Even the food price inflation as measured by STATS SA is not reflective of the actual rand price increases that especially the poor are experiencing.

VO: Economist Lesiba Mothata highlights that overall wage increases and the rate of inflation are not keeping up with one another

Lesiba: On average wage growth in the country for those that are in the in the private sector has been 4.5%. we find that inflation peaked around 6.8% and that mismatch is concluded by a consumer who is not able to afford a lot more things.

Viccy: Baby formula has become a precious commodity, Its being stolen from stores so they're having to put security tags around it like they way that they do with alcohol and things like that.


We used to buy a specific brand of baby formula when our son Senna was born two years ago, then it cost R170,00 and now it costs R290,00

Viccy: One gram of baby formula costs almost R2

VO: Viccy Baker from Price Watch gathers data on food and grocery prices from 10 different centers around South Africa.

Viccy: Everything that's on the shelf that is something that you'd put into your grocery basket, we track.

VO: Due to severe drought last year Carte Blanche reported that food prices could increase up to 30% by April this year.
According to the PACSA food barometer prices did rise substantially peaking at around 27% in January 2017, stretching everyone's budgets even more.

Vuyo: What it means for a family when they run out of money is the fact that they have to survive for basically next to nothing.

So you are finding a situation where people are basically living on carbohydrates, which actually does nothing for what's required for basic nutrition.

VO: Sibongile Khumalo, a mother of two is the sole supporter for her family, she earns her living from part time cleaning work, and receives social grants for her children of R380,00 each. Sibongile averages a total income of around R2500,00 per month, but now she says her income is worth even less than last year.

Sibongile: I used to buy eggs like 60 like I used to buy big big big, now like I buy like 18 smaller smaller smaller even the fish oil, now its expensive.

Vuyo: For instance from December last year to march now, it would have cost in Gauteng an average R10 for 6 eggs and now it costs up to R15.

VO: So often Sibongile's food supply simply runs out. This is the food her family has left half way through the month.

Sibongile: We can have 3 times a day, meal, like breakfast, there is bread, we buy egg and we make and porridge, but after one week everything is gone we just make porridge, we eat the pup or rice that is yesterday in the lunch.

VO: PACSA tracks a food basket of 36 basic food items that low-income households normally buy. The increase on this basket year on year is 10.6%, which falls in line with the STATS SA food inflation rate of 9.9% for 2017, but this does not necessarily reflect the real hidden cost of food especially on low-income families.

Julie: For most black SA households on lower baseline wages, they have cut back to a point where they cant cut back any further without severe devastating consequences.

VO: The PACSA food barometer indicates that the cost of “big foods”, staple starches like maize, rice and beans has increased by 29% since November 2015 and this makes up 36% of the basket.

Julie: It means there's less money to spend on meats, proteins, dairy It has a severe impact on the nutrition of families but particularly women because they eat last.

Sibongile: Like when I see like the food like I cook maybe the rice it was little bit I just cook I dish out for them, I just sleep, but I am not feeling hungry.

VO: Our death statistics show that women between the ages of 45 and 64 suffer the consequences of poor nutrition with non communicable diseases being the highest causes of death.

Sibongile: My food, its not balanced, because I cant afford to buy what I am concentrating is rent school fees.

Vuyo: Where it has become inconceivable to have three meals a day, you can't live in dignity when you're constantly struggling to survive and constantly surviving to struggle

Bongani: Drought, a fluctuating currency, now downgrades, all of these factors have combined to put our economy under severe pressure and nowhere has this been felt more than at the tills, so is there any release in store for consumers?

We had to compromise chicken or mince meat, we used to buy a lot with R600, we can only buy two kgs.

Other food items that are basics, dairy yoghurts, from 18,99 to 30,00 its astronomical

Vicccy Some particular chicken cuts their prices has gone up by more than 30% y/y

What is happening is that the price is going up and the size of the frozen chicken bag is going down. So what was 5kg is now 4.2kg, So you're paying more and you're getting less.

Lesiba: The retail level its really that which the consumer puts in a trolley and pushes to pay at the tellers. so that price has began to come down but it is not fast enough. It’s held up by meat prices which are sticky coming down.

VO: Economists had predicted a possible decrease in food inflation to 7.4% by the 3rd quarter this year, but a reported looming El Ninho within the next 24 months could send us into another drought and South Africa's downgrade to junk status by two ratings agencies has severely jeopardised this decrease.

Tinashe: The downgrade led to a significant weakening of the exchange rate. What it means, now you are paying roughly 10% more on your input costs than what you were paying before the downgrade happened. [

Lesiba: We were looking at a growth rate of around 1.3% in GDP. Now with this downgrade and everything else around confidence that is weakening, it could actually result with a GDP growth that looks a lot more like 2016.

VO: But it's not only the poor that are in trouble. Interest rates are predicted to rise and the middle classes have a lot of debt to service.

Tinashe: you have a weakening of the buying power of the middle class. because a weakening rand means you are getting poorer. We are probably 10% poorer than we were.

VO: But in reality it is far worse. In order to feed a child a nutritious meal it would cost R20,89 per day, as compared to a child living off a grant which works out to R12,67 per day. In essence that is 39% less food on the plates of 12 million children.

Julie: That has severe, immediate consequences around cognitive development, around the ability of kids to learn and play and grow

Sibongile: Even the pup I eat I don't eat that it takes a lot of milie meal, I eat the pup you just pour you mix it then its fine, I am not eating the heavy pup.

VO: Even though the picture may appear bleak, it doesn't necessarily mean that we can't change and adapt our lifestyles and our approach to food security.

Tinashe Over the next 20 years, 16 million young South Africans will enter the labour force. It's almost doubling the labour force. It almost means we have to double the GDP.

Lesiba: What needs to happen is to grow the labour force base, have a lot more people working so that they can stay on their own feet and create opportunities for themselves.

Julie: We all want to ensure that SA transforms to make sure that everybody is included
FIN

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): An estimated fourteen million South Africans are going to bed hungry everyday. Economists are projecting a turn for the better with food prices, but is that a reality at the tills?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The turn of the year 2017 has shown positive signs of food prices dropping in South Africa with economists projecting the food inflation to decline up to 7% by midyear. Consumers however, still have to dig deep into their pockets to put food on the table with prices of basic nutritional staples not reflecting the anticipated consumer relief at the supermarkets while the poor, in fact, are further stifled.
metadata.Summary: Severe draught, the weakening Rand and an increased rate of imported foods have all plagued the South African food economy in the past two years. The cost of food prices climbed to almost 30% in 2016, putting ordinary South Africans against the ropes just to feed their families. A good rain spell in the recent months has however improved the Agricultural sector in South Africa with Grain industry expected to produce a surplus in 2017. This will help reduce the price of food products such as maize, which is a major staple, particularly in low- income households. Maize has already shown a downtrend since January 2017 and this is expected to impact majorly on food inflation in South Africa and consumers are supposed to be feeling the decrease already. On the contrary the general projection of food inflation has risen by 10% y/y in South Africans and consumers are still paying more for a basic nutritional diet in their house with other staples such as meat, sugar and cooking oil still at an all time high. The recent downgrade of our economy to junk status coupled with the less 5% salary increases across the working class and the social grants, maintains a gloomy picture for the consumer, especially the poor. In this follow up piece, we unpack the discrepancy between the positive economic outlook and the negative reality hitting the consumer at the super markets. Experts shed light on what is influencing the current food inflation and what the ordinary South African consumer should brace them selves for.
metadata.Further information: According to world bank surveys, South Africa is one of the most unequal societies in the world, sitting at number 2, when it comes to poverty and inequality, with our CEO's being the 7th highest paid globally. Vuyokazi from SPII (Studies in Poverty and Inequality Institute) puts into perspective what an average low incomme household and ones that rely on social grants spend on food. Based on their research, how does inflation work against a social grant recipient whom their annual increase does not equate to the annual increases in food inflation.” The standard of living the poor are expected to live on is degrading” She backs this up the Trend Analysis of essential food and non-food basket they conduct at the SPII. Last year we tracked the food basket from PACSA nutritional basket in 2016. Julie Smith from PACSA outlines how their food basket of nutritional and non-nutritional food items has increased on a m/m basis as well as y/y to date. Julie also breaks down the inadequacy of the suggested national minimum wage of R3500 by government compared to the cost of a nutritional food basket of a family consisting of five people according to the PACSA research and food barometer. To unpack this at a broader economic level, economist, Lesiba Mothata from Investment Solutions, talks to us about the general effect of inflation on the middle class and low-income earners. Lesiba also unpacks the level of inequality in South Africa and why especially the low-income household will feel the brunt of an economic downgrade in the country. Who will absorb the high interest rates in the country now that we are at a junk status? Most importantly Lesiba will put into perspective on a larger scale the reason why the supposed decline and positive outlook on food inflation doesn’t reflect at the shops for the consumer. Viccy Baker of Price Watch believes there is a discrepancy in the increases of certain foods from certain brands. According to Viccy some of the brands’ are unnecessarily high and the rate in which they increase suggests price fixing and profiteering. She takes us on stroll in the supermarket as she discusses some of the foods she used to buy for cheaper and they have since accelerated to almost twice their former price. Based on the food items they track at Price Watch, she helps us compare the national statistics and inflation rates to what they have calculated. In conclusion, the experts, Wandile and Lesiba give us an actual figure breakdown of what the food inflation projection is standing at and also a little advice for the consumer and whether they should be more cautious with their spending, or better days are near. What is the forecast for the near future, is it positive, or are factors such as an economic downgrade going send back to a 20%+ food inflation rate?
